title: What Can Go Wrong, Written Down: A Hazard Log, a Risk Matrix and the Rule That a Catastrophe Is Never Low

questions.question: Why keep a hazard log from the start of a project and not at the end?
options: A log started late has fewer entries, and a short log is quicker to review
The standard requires the log to be dated before the first line of code
Hazards cannot be scored until the machine has been built and measured
A safeguard nobody wrote a hazard for cannot be shown to cover anything, and hazards found late are expensive to answer
questions.explanation: Each safeguard is an answer to a hazard. Without the hazard written down first, nobody can say what a safeguard is for, or what has been left with none.

questions.question: Severity 4 with likelihood 1 scores 4. By the product alone that is low. What does the log class it as?
options: Medium: a catastrophic outcome is never classed below medium, because the likelihood is a guess and the outcome is not
Low: 4 is in the low band, and the class follows the score
High: any severity 4 is at least high
Unacceptable: a possible death can never be accepted
questions.explanation: The likelihood is an estimate made by people who hope it is small. The severity is what happens. So one rule overrides the product: severity 4 never classes below medium.

questions.question: A hazard is added with no id, severity 9 and no owner. What does add answer?
options: no_id: the checks are made in a fixed order and the first failure is the answer, and nothing is kept
bad_severity: the worst fault is reported first
no_owner: the owner is checked before anything else
ok, with the missing fields filled by defaults
questions.explanation: The checks run in a fixed order, id first, and the first failure is the answer. A refused hazard is not kept half way.

questions.question: Two hazards both score 12, one at severity 4 and likelihood 3 and one at severity 3 and likelihood 4. Which is ranked first?
options: The second: a likelihood of 4 means it will happen sooner
Either: equal scores have no order
The first: ties break by severity, then by id, so the catastrophic one leads and the order is always the same
Whichever was added to the log first
questions.explanation: Two hazards at 12 are not equal risks. The tie goes to the higher severity, and then to the id, so the list is the same on every machine.

questions.question: unaddressed() lists a severity 4, likelihood 1 fire with no mitigation but not a severity 2, likelihood 1 pinch with none. Why?
options: The pinch has an owner and the fire has none
The fire is medium by the floor and so is not low, while the pinch is low: a low risk with nothing done is allowed, a catastrophe with nothing done is not
The fire scores higher than the pinch by the product
The pinch has a mitigation that the log does not show
questions.explanation: Both score low by the product. The floor lifts the fire to medium, and anything that is not low needs something done about it.

questions.question: Eight ground vehicle hazards scored 1 unacceptable, 3 high and 4 medium. Which was the unacceptable one?
options: Running into a person, scoring 12
Keeping on driving when the link is lost, scoring 16: the reason for an independent stop path
Rolling over on a slope, scoring 9
A sensor failing with nothing noticing, scoring 12
questions.explanation: A machine that drives on with nothing in control of it was the only one at 15 or more. The next lesson is its answer.
